screens.title: Working with Amazon DynamoDB — Core Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of Amazon DynamoDB and why teams choose it for serverless, high-throughput systems. DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database. That means it favors flexible schemas, horizontal scale, and single-digit millisecond performance over the rigid structure and joins of relational databases. You’ll learn the vocabulary — tables, items, attributes — and the single most important design decision: choosing the primary key. We will compare a simple partition key to a composite primary key, and see how that choice affects queries, cost, and performance. You’ll also learn the two capacity modes — provisioned and on-demand — and when each is appropriate. Finally, we’ll preview practical work: creating a simple Movies table, performing create, read, update, and delete operations with the AWS SDK for Python, and spotting common mistakes like hot partitions or overreliance on scans. By the end you should be able to pick a primary key that supports your access patterns and choose a capacity mode that fits expected traffic. Consider how a social feed or a game backend would store frequent events; that concrete design question will guide everything we do next.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will have four practical competencies you can verify in real projects. First, you will distinguish a relational database from a NoSQL store like DynamoDB. That means recognizing when a flexible item-based model and horizontal scaling make sense. Second, you'll be able to explain tables, items, and attributes in DynamoDB terms and map those to entities in your application. Third, you will understand the role of primary keys — both simple partition keys and composite keys with sort keys — and why that decision affects query performance and data distribution. Fourth, you'll practice using the AWS SDK to perform create, read, update, and delete operations, so you can prototype a simple application backend. Each objective links a conceptual skill to a small practical check: explain the model to a teammate, design a table schema, write a query using a key condition, and run a short script that adds and retrieves items. These abilities will let you design low-latency data access patterns and avoid common mistakes like hot partitions or inefficient scans.

screens.title: NoSQL vs Relational — The design trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring what we mean by NoSQL in practice. A relational database enforces a fixed schema, normalized tables, and joins. This is excellent for complex transactions and strong relationships, but it can be limiting if your data evolves often or your access patterns prioritize key-value lookups. DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value and document database: it stores items that can each have different attributes, and it focuses on predictable, low-latency reads and writes at any scale. That flexibility matters when building mobile backends, game leaderboards, IoT event stores, or ad-tech where new attributes appear frequently or where high throughput is required. A common misconception is to think NoSQL means unstructured chaos; in reality, good NoSQL design is deliberate: you model your table around access patterns rather than purely around relations. For example, a user profile item may include username, email, preferences and nested objects for settings without requiring an alter table call. Contrast that with a relational migration workflow. A practical check: if your application frequently needs range queries or aggregations across many related entities, a relational model may still be appropriate. If you need massive scale and simple, predictable access by key, DynamoDB is often a better fit. Keep asking: which queries must be fast and how will data grow? That question drives whether to use a flexible item model or a relational schema.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: NoSQL stores like DynamoDB favor flexible schemas and key-based access; choose the model based on access patterns, not familiarity.

content.html:
Definition

Relational vs NoSQL

Relational: fixed schema, joins, good for strong consistency and complex transactions. NoSQL (DynamoDB): flexible item attributes and scale for key-value and document patterns.

When to choose DynamoDB
High throughput, low latency, evolving attributes, simple access by key.
Misconception
NoSQL is not schema-less chaos — you design for access patterns.
Key Takeaway

Pick DynamoDB when your reads and writes are dominated by key-based access patterns and you need predictable latency at scale.

Analogy

Analogy: Library vs Filing cabinet

A relational database is like a library index with cross-references. DynamoDB is like many filing cabinets keyed by a label you know in advance.

Example Scenario
Game leaderboard
Store player records with dynamic attributes like achievements and last_seen. Fast reads and writes per player favor DynamoDB.
Common Mistake
Designing schema without mapping queries first leads to noisy scans and high cost.

screens.title: Tables, Items, and Attributes — The data model
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB organizes data in a simple three-level hierarchy: tables, items, and attributes. Think of a table as a named collection of items that represent entities in your application. Each item is like a row, but crucially items do not have to share the same set of attributes. Attributes are the properties of an item, comparable to columns in a relational table but optional and flexible. This lets you store nested documents or varying fields per item without migrations. For example, a Movies table could contain items where some entries have an info block with plot and rating while others omit those fields. Every item must include the attributes that form its primary key so it can be uniquely identified. When modeling your application, map entities and their primary access patterns to this hierarchy first: what will you query by, and which data must come back with the item? Avoid modeling purely as normalized entities; instead, denormalize for efficient reads when necessary. A common design sequence is: identify the core entity (table), decide what uniquely identifies it (primary key), then list optional attributes and nested objects you will store. This structured approach helps you predict performance, limits the need for scans, and simplifies client code.

keyIdea.title: Data model
keyIdea.text: Tables contain items; items contain attributes. Items are flexible so you design for access patterns rather than strict schemas.

content.html:
Hierarchy

Tables • Items • Attributes

Map your application entities into tables, pick items that represent single entities, and list attributes you need returned by queries.

Table
Named container for items, e.g., Movies.
Item
One entity; attributes may vary per item.
Attribute
Property of an item. Required only if part of the key.
Practical rule
  • Decide which queries must be fast and ensure the key supports them.
  • Denormalize when it reduces read complexity and cost.
  • Keep items small when possible to reduce RCU/WCU usage.
Example
Movies table
Item: { year: 2015, title: "The Big New Movie", info: { plot: "Nothing happens.", rating: 0 } }
Key Takeaway

Model tables by the entities you need to query and list attributes that must be returned to avoid extra calls.

screens.title: Primary Keys — Partition Key design
screens.narratorSegment: The partition key is fundamental to how DynamoDB stores items. DynamoDB applies an internal hash function to the partition key value to choose a storage partition for that item. A good partition key yields an even distribution of items across partitions. If you pick a value that clusters many writes or reads on a small set of keys, you create a hot partition and risk throttling. Start by listing your application's most frequent access patterns. If you're storing user profiles and most operations target a single user by id, then user_id is a natural partition key. For time-series or ordered data, avoid using a strictly increasing value as the partition key, because new items will target the same partition. A practical design process: 1) list top queries, 2) propose candidate partition keys, 3) estimate cardinality and request distribution for each candidate, and 4) pick the key that spreads load and supports fast GetItem queries. Remember that a partition key alone creates a simple primary key that is ideal for single-item retrieval by key. If you need ordered queries inside a partition, consider a composite primary key with a sort key, which we will cover next. The misconception to avoid is thinking only about uniqueness; distribution and access pattern alignment are equally important.

keyIdea.title: Partition Key
keyIdea.text: Partition key hashes to storage; choose a key with high cardinality and evenly distributed access to avoid hot partitions.

content.html:
Process Flow

Designing a Partition Key

1.
List frequent queries and the access pattern for reads and writes.
2.
Propose candidate keys and estimate cardinality and traffic distribution.
3.
Prefer keys that spread load; avoid sequential timestamps as partition keys.
4.
Choose the key that enables GetItem or Query for the top access patterns.
Key Takeaway

Good partition key design balances uniqueness and access distribution to prevent throttling and hot partitions.

Example
User profiles: partition key = user_id. For orders where you need ordering by date, a composite key is better. Avoid using an ever-increasing counter as the partition key because writes will cluster.
Common Mistake
Choosing low-cardinality keys that place most traffic on a few partitions.

screens.title: Composite Primary Key — Partition + Sort Key
screens.narratorSegment: A composite primary key adds a sort key to the partition key. All items that share the same partition key are stored together and ordered by the sort key. This structure enables efficient range queries within a partition, such as fetching all orders for a user between two dates. The key idea is grouping: use the partition key to gather related items and the sort key to order or filter them. For example, design a table with partition key user_id and sort key order_date to retrieve a user's orders in date order with a single Query operation. Query supports range conditions on the sort key, so you can request items between date A and date B without scanning the whole table. A common misconception is that you should add a sort key whenever you need sorting; instead add it only when access patterns require grouping by the same partition and range filters. Also be mindful of write patterns: if many writes target the same partition and sort key range, you can still create hotspots within that partition. The composite key is a powerful tool when you want denormalized, ordered collections grouped by a natural partition such as a user or device identifier.

keyIdea.title: Composite Key
keyIdea.text: Use a partition key to group related items and a sort key to order or filter them efficiently with Query operations.

content.html:
Comparison

Partition Key vs Composite Key

Partition only
Good for single-item GetItem lookups by unique id.
Composite
Group and order items within a partition; supports range queries on the sort key.
Query benefit
Querying by partition with sort conditions reads only the matching partition's items.
Example
Orders table
Partition key: user_id. Sort key: order_date. Query returns orders for a user between two dates.
Common Pitfall
Using a composite key without planning for partition cardinality can cluster writes from many users into few partitions if the partition value has low cardinality.
Check Your Understanding
If you need to retrieve all login sessions for a user sorted by login_time, which key design fits best? (Partition: user_id, Sort: login_time)

screens.title: Hot Partitions — Causes and Mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: A hot partition occurs when a disproportionate amount of read or write traffic targets a small set of partition key values. Because DynamoDB assigns throughput capacity at the partition level, that imbalance can cause throttling and degraded performance even when the table's overall capacity looks sufficient. Common causes include using a timestamp or monotonically increasing id as a partition key, low-cardinality keys like a country code, or a single popular item that receives most writes. To diagnose a hot partition, examine CloudWatch metrics and request patterns and see if a few partition key values account for most operations. Mitigation strategies include reshaping the key to increase cardinality, adding a prefix or suffix that shards the key across values, or moving to On-Demand capacity to absorb short bursts while you redesign. Another common pattern is to use composite keys with an additional dimension that distributes writes. Remember, a fix that increases cardinality must still support your read access patterns; do not shard keys in a way that makes queries harder. The central principle: design keys with both uniqueness and predictable distribution in mind.

keyIdea.title: Hot Partition
keyIdea.text: Hot partitions arise from uneven access; mitigate by increasing cardinality, sharding keys, or adjusting capacity until you redesign.

content.html:
Core Concept

Hot Partitions: diagnosis and fixes

Cause: low-cardinality or sequential partition values concentrate requests.
Diagnose: CloudWatch per-partition metrics, request logs, or throttling patterns show concentrated keys.
Fixes: redesign key to increase cardinality, add a sharding prefix/suffix, or use On-Demand as a short-term buffer.
Trade-off: sharding adds complexity for reads; balance distribution against query simplicity.
Example
If you use timestamp as partition key, all writes go to the newest partition and create a hotspot.
Mitigation Cards
Increase key cardinality by adding user-scoped id parts.
Shard by hash prefix when writes concentrate on one value.
Temporary: use On-Demand to absorb variable bursts while redesigning.

screens.title: Provisioned vs On-Demand Capacity Modes
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB offers two capacity modes that control how you provision throughput. Provisioned capacity requires you to set read and write capacity units. This model is cost-efficient for predictable workloads because you can provision just what you need and enable Auto Scaling to adjust capacity over time. Understand the units: a write capacity unit generally covers one write per second for an item up to 1 KB; read capacity units vary depending on read consistency and item size. On the other hand, On-Demand capacity charges per request and automatically scales to accommodate traffic spikes, which makes it ideal for new or unpredictable workloads. The trade-off is cost: On-Demand can be more expensive for consistently high traffic. A common design pattern is to start with On-Demand during early development or irregular traffic, and switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling once you understand patterns. Also consider mixed strategies with separate tables for unpredictable workloads. Avoid guessing capacity numbers; use metrics to measure and plan. The practical decision comes down to predictability, budget, and your willingness to operate Auto Scaling policies. Provisioned vs On-Demand Capacity Modes means provisioned is cost-effective for predictable traffic; on-demand is simpler for unknown or spiky workloads — measure and choose accordingly.. In practical terms, choosing the right throughput model for cost and traffic patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Provisioned is cost-effective for predictable traffic; On-Demand is simpler for unknown or spiky workloads — measure and choose accordingly.

content.html:
Comparison

Provisioned vs On-Demand

Provisioned: Specify RCU/WCU, use Auto Scaling, good for predictable workloads.
On-Demand: Pay per request, no capacity planning, good for unpredictable spikes or early development.
Practical Advice

Start On-Demand for unpredictable traffic, measure usage, then consider Provisioned with Auto Scaling if costs justify optimization.

Example Scenarios
  • New product launch: On-Demand to avoid underprovisioning.
  • Stable backend with known peak: Provisioned with Auto Scaling to lower cost.
  • Mixed workloads: separate tables per access pattern to control costs.

screens.title: CRUD with Boto3 — Create and PutItem
screens.narratorSegment: Now we get practical with code. Using Boto3 you can create a table and add items with a few A P I calls. The provided Movies example creates a table with a composite key: year as the partition key and title as the sort key. When creating a table, you declare the KeySchema and AttributeDefinitions — the attribute types matter for how DynamoDB stores and indexes items. In the code sample we use BillingMode set to pay per request to keep setup simple. After the table exists, put_item adds a new item and requires the full primary key attributes in the item. This operation is atomic for that item. A common misconception is assuming a put_item can partially update nested attributes — put_item replaces or writes the full item. For partial updates use update_item with an UpdateExpression. As a developer, you should test create_table, wait until the table exists, and then run put_item and get_item to verify the stored attributes. In a real project, add error handling for resource already exists and client errors. Later screens walk through get, update, and delete operations and show how Query and Scan differ in cost and use.

Code Walkthrough

Create table and add items (Boto3)

Key points: specify KeySchema and AttributeDefinitions; BillingMode can be PAY_PER_REQUEST for On-Demand simplicity.
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='us-east-1')

# Create table
try:
  table = dynamodb.create_table(
    TableName='Movies',
    KeySchema=[
      {'AttributeName': 'year', 'KeyType': 'HASH'},
      {'AttributeName': 'title', 'KeyType': 'RANGE'}
    ],
    AttributeDefinitions=[
      {'AttributeName': 'year', 'AttributeType': 'N'},
      {'AttributeName': 'title', 'AttributeType': 'S'}
    ],
    BillingMode='PAY_PER_REQUEST'
  )
  table.wait_until_exists()
except ClientError as e:
  if e.response['Error']['Code'] == 'ResourceInUseException':
    table = dynamodb.Table('Movies')
Example
Add items using put_item. put_item replaces the item with the provided attributes — use update_item for partial changes.
def add_movie(year, title, info):
  table = dynamodb.Table('Movies')
  try:
    response = table.put_item(Item={'year': year, 'title': title, 'info': info})
    return response
  except ClientError as e:
    raise
Key Takeaway

Use create_table and put_item to provision and populate a table; verify items with get_item to ensure key attributes are stored correctly.

GetItem is the most efficient read because it requires the full primary key. It returns a single item or nothing. Use Query when you need multiple items sharing a partition key and optional sort key conditions. For updates, update_item uses UpdateExpression to change only specified attributes rather than replacing the whole item; it returns updated attributes when requested. DeleteItem removes an item by its primary key. In practice, always handle ClientError exceptions and consider conditional expressions to prevent accidental overwrites or deletions. For example, include a condition that an attribute exists or a version matches before updating. A common misconception is to expect update_item to create missing parent structures in nested maps automatically — you must explicitly set them in the expression. Also be mindful of item size and return values to control RCU/WCU consumption. After an update, use get_item to verify the change or rely on ReturnValues from update_item for confirmation. Proper error handling and conditional writes help maintain data integrity in concurrent environments. content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Get, Update, Delete examples

def get_movie(year, title):
  table = dynamodb.Table('Movies')
  try:
    response = table.get_item(Key={'year': year, 'title': title})
    return response.get('Item')
  except ClientError as e:
    raise

def update_movie(year, title, rating):
  table = dynamodb.Table('Movies')
  try:
    response = table.update_item(
      Key={'year': year, 'title': title},
      UpdateExpression='SET info.rating = :val',
      ExpressionAttributeValues={':val': rating},
      ReturnValues='UPDATED_NEW'
    )
    return response
  except ClientError as e:
    raise

def delete_movie(year, title):
  table = dynamodb.Table('Movies')
  try:
    response = table.delete_item(Key={'year': year, 'title': title})
    return response
  except ClientError as e:
    raise
Guidance
  • Prefer GetItem for single-item reads; Query for multiple items within a partition.
  • Use conditional expressions to prevent race conditions when updating or deleting.
  • Request ReturnValues when you need confirmation of an update rather than a follow-up GetItem.
Key Takeaway

Use GetItem and Query for efficient reads, UpdateExpression for partial item updates, and conditional writes to protect integrity.

screens.title: Query vs Scan — Performance and cost differences
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between Query and Scan is essential for cost and performance. Query retrieves items that share a partition key and optionally filters by sort key conditions. Because Query targets a specific partition, it reads only the necessary items, making it efficient and cost-effective. Scan reads every item in the table or a secondary index and then applies any filters, which can result in high read throughput and large costs on big tables. Use Scan primarily for small tables, one-time operations, or administrative tasks where cost is acceptable. If you need to support flexible access patterns that would otherwise require scans, consider introducing secondary indexes or redesigning your data model to support those queries efficiently. A common misconception is that adding a filter to a Query is the same as a Scan — filters applied after Query still only operate on items returned by the partition-scope request, while Scan always examines the entire table. In short, prefer GetItem and Query for predictable performance and reserve Scan for exceptional cases or small datasets. content.html:
Comparison

Query vs Scan

Query: Efficient, requires partition key, supports sort key range filters.
Scan: Inefficient for large tables since it examines every item; filters are post-read operations.
When to use Scan
Small tables, initial data migrations, or administrative inspections when cost is acceptable.
Practical Tips
  • Prefer Query/GetItem for production reads to reduce cost and latency.
  • If you need additional access patterns, use secondary indexes or denormalize data.
  • Paginate large scans and monitor RCU usage closely.
Key Takeaway

Design for Queryable patterns. Replace Scan-based reads with targeted indexes or denormalized structures when possible.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's close by reinforcing three essential concepts. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of Amazon DynamoDB and why teams choose it for serverless, high-throughput systems. DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database. That means it favors flexible schemas, horizontal scale, and single-digit millisecond performance over the rigid structure and joins of relational databases. You’ll learn the vocabulary — tables, items, attributes — and the single most important design decision: choosing the primary key. We will compare a simple partition key to a composite primary key, and see how that choice affects queries, cost, and performance. You’ll also learn the two capacity modes — provisioned and on-demand — and when each is appropriate. Finally, we’ll preview practical work: creating a simple Movies table, performing create, read, update, and delete operations with the AWS SDK for Python, and spotting common mistakes like hot partitions or overreliance on scans. By the end you should be able to pick a primary key that supports your access patterns and choose a capacity mode that fits expected traffic. Consider how a social feed or a game backend would store frequent events; that concrete design question will guide everything we do next.

By the end of these lessons you will have four practical competencies you can verify in real projects. First, you will distinguish a relational database from a NoSQL store like DynamoDB. That means recognizing when a flexible item-based model and horizontal scaling make sense. Second, you'll be able to explain tables, items, and attributes in DynamoDB terms and map those to entities in your application. Third, you will understand the role of primary keys — both simple partition keys and composite keys with sort keys — and why that decision affects query performance and data distribution. Fourth, you'll practice using the AWS SDK to perform create, read, update, and delete operations, so you can prototype a simple application backend. Each objective links a conceptual skill to a small practical check: explain the model to a teammate, design a table schema, write a query using a key condition, and run a short script that adds and retrieves items. These abilities will let you design low-latency data access patterns and avoid common mistakes like hot partitions or inefficient scans.

This second objectives screen links concepts to small design tasks you can practice. You'll learn to select a primary key that supports frequent access patterns — for example, using user_id plus login_time as a composite key to fetch user sessions efficiently. You'll explore capacity mode decisions: choose provisioned with auto scaling for predictable workloads, or On-Demand when traffic is unpredictable. You'll practice spotting hot partitions and redesigning keys to improve distribution. Finally, you'll contrast Query and Scan operations and learn to prefer GetItem or Query for cost and performance. Each objective pairs with a tiny lab action: design a table schema on paper, run the provided Python script to create and manipulate a Movies table, inspect the DynamoDB console, and add a query function to the script. These tasks bridge knowledge and practice so you can make design choices with confidence and avoid common pitfalls in production systems.

Start by anchoring what we mean by NoSQL in practice. A relational database enforces a fixed schema, normalized tables, and joins. This is excellent for complex transactions and strong relationships, but it can be limiting if your data evolves often or your access patterns prioritize key-value lookups. DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value and document database: it stores items that can each have different attributes, and it focuses on predictable, low-latency reads and writes at any scale. That flexibility matters when building mobile backends, game leaderboards, IoT event stores, or ad-tech where new attributes appear frequently or where high throughput is required. A common misconception is to think NoSQL means unstructured chaos; in reality, good NoSQL design is deliberate: you model your table around access patterns rather than purely around relations. For example, a user profile item may include username, email, preferences and nested objects for settings without requiring an alter table call. Contrast that with a relational migration workflow. A practical check: if your application frequently needs range queries or aggregations across many related entities, a relational model may still be appropriate. If you need massive scale and simple, predictable access by key, DynamoDB is often a better fit. Keep asking: which queries must be fast and how will data grow? That question drives whether to use a flexible item model or a relational schema.

DynamoDB organizes data in a simple three-level hierarchy: tables, items, and attributes. Think of a table as a named collection of items that represent entities in your application. Each item is like a row, but crucially items do not have to share the same set of attributes. Attributes are the properties of an item, comparable to columns in a relational table but optional and flexible. This lets you store nested documents or varying fields per item without migrations. For example, a Movies table could contain items where some entries have an info block with plot and rating while others omit those fields. Every item must include the attributes that form its primary key so it can be uniquely identified. When modeling your application, map entities and their primary access patterns to this hierarchy first: what will you query by, and which data must come back with the item? Avoid modeling purely as normalized entities; instead, denormalize for efficient reads when necessary. A common design sequence is: identify the core entity (table), decide what uniquely identifies it (primary key), then list optional attributes and nested objects you will store. This structured approach helps you predict performance, limits the need for scans, and simplifies client code.

The partition key is fundamental to how DynamoDB stores items. DynamoDB applies an internal hash function to the partition key value to choose a storage partition for that item. A good partition key yields an even distribution of items across partitions. If you pick a value that clusters many writes or reads on a small set of keys, you create a hot partition and risk throttling. Start by listing your application's most frequent access patterns. If you're storing user profiles and most operations target a single user by id, then user_id is a natural partition key. For time-series or ordered data, avoid using a strictly increasing value as the partition key, because new items will target the same partition. A practical design process: 1) list top queries, 2) propose candidate partition keys, 3) estimate cardinality and request distribution for each candidate, and 4) pick the key that spreads load and supports fast GetItem queries. Remember that a partition key alone creates a simple primary key that is ideal for single-item retrieval by key. If you need ordered queries inside a partition, consider a composite primary key with a sort key, which we will cover next. The misconception to avoid is thinking only about uniqueness; distribution and access pattern alignment are equally important.

A composite primary key adds a sort key to the partition key. All items that share the same partition key are stored together and ordered by the sort key. This structure enables efficient range queries within a partition, such as fetching all orders for a user between two dates. The key idea is grouping: use the partition key to gather related items and the sort key to order or filter them. For example, design a table with partition key user_id and sort key order_date to retrieve a user's orders in date order with a single Query operation. Query supports range conditions on the sort key, so you can request items between date A and date B without scanning the whole table. A common misconception is that you should add a sort key whenever you need sorting; instead add it only when access patterns require grouping by the same partition and range filters. Also be mindful of write patterns: if many writes target the same partition and sort key range, you can still create hotspots within that partition. The composite key is a powerful tool when you want denormalized, ordered collections grouped by a natural partition such as a user or device identifier.

A hot partition occurs when a disproportionate amount of read or write traffic targets a small set of partition key values. Because DynamoDB assigns throughput capacity at the partition level, that imbalance can cause throttling and degraded performance even when the table's overall capacity looks sufficient. Common causes include using a timestamp or monotonically increasing id as a partition key, low-cardinality keys like a country code, or a single popular item that receives most writes. To diagnose a hot partition, examine CloudWatch metrics and request patterns and see if a few partition key values account for most operations. Mitigation strategies include reshaping the key to increase cardinality, adding a prefix or suffix that shards the key across values, or moving to On-Demand capacity to absorb short bursts while you redesign. Another common pattern is to use composite keys with an additional dimension that distributes writes. Remember, a fix that increases cardinality must still support your read access patterns; do not shard keys in a way that makes queries harder. The central principle: design keys with both uniqueness and predictable distribution in mind.

DynamoDB offers two capacity modes that control how you provision throughput. Provisioned capacity requires you to set read and write capacity units. This model is cost-efficient for predictable workloads because you can provision just what you need and enable Auto Scaling to adjust capacity over time. Understand the units: a write capacity unit generally covers one write per second for an item up to 1 KB; read capacity units vary depending on read consistency and item size. On the other hand, On-Demand capacity charges per request and automatically scales to accommodate traffic spikes, which makes it ideal for new or unpredictable workloads. The trade-off is cost: On-Demand can be more expensive for consistently high traffic. A common design pattern is to start with On-Demand during early development or irregular traffic, and switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling once you understand patterns. Also consider mixed strategies with separate tables for unpredictable workloads. Avoid guessing capacity numbers; use metrics to measure and plan. The practical decision comes down to predictability, budget, and your willingness to operate Auto Scaling policies. Provisioned vs On-Demand Capacity Modes means provisioned is cost-effective for predictable traffic; on-demand is simpler for unknown or spiky workloads — measure and choose accordingly.. In practical terms, choosing the right throughput model for cost and traffic patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

First, DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL key-value and document store that favors flexible items and predictable low-latency access, so choose it when your access patterns are dominated by key-based reads and writes. Second, primary key design is central: the partition key determines physical distribution and a composite key with a sort key enables efficient range queries within a partition. Think carefully about cardinality and access patterns to avoid hot partitions. Third, capacity mode matters: use On-Demand for unpredictable traffic or early development, and adopt Provisioned capacity with Auto Scaling for predictable workloads to optimize cost. Also remember practical A P I patterns: prefer GetItem and Query for efficiency, use UpdateExpression for partial updates, and avoid Scan on large tables. These points together will guide your table schema and runtime choices and help you build scalable, cost-aware services.
